# Independent audit: planar midpoint-component closure

Auditor: research-agent. Date: 2026-09-20.

**PASS** for

    candidate 965c1fac7900f6cc

The theorem is correctly restricted to components of affine lattice rank at most two. It neither repairs the rank-three obstruction nor gives a depth bound.

## Key checks

1. Integer points on a segment between two component points form a chain of consecutive primitive steps. Consecutive triples join the entire chain when it has an interior point. Hence boundary-edge points cannot be missing from a planar component's hull.

2. A minimum-area nondegenerate triangle in a midpoint-closed rank-two component cannot have two same-parity vertices: their integral midpoint lies in the component and halves the triangle's area. Thus the component uses at least three of the plane lattice's four parity classes.

3. In \(T=\operatorname{conv}(C)\cap\mathbb Z^2\), all missing points have the one remaining parity class. Their midpoint cannot belong to \(C\), since that would join them to \(C\). A closest distinct pair therefore contradicts closure under taking its strictly closer midpoint. Thus at most one point \(q\) is missing. It is isolated in \(T\), even if its original component in a larger set extends outside this hull. All connecting paths of \(C\) are retained because their vertices already lie in \(C\).

4. The isolated point must be interior. The source's classification of an isolated interior point is fully proved, rather than cited from a polygon list. A smallest integer-vertex triangle strictly containing \(q\) has no additional lattice point: any such point subdivides it into smaller triangles, or puts \(q\) in the relative interior of an integer segment, which would give an integral midpoint through \(q\).

5. Each of the three subtriangles from \(q\) is empty and therefore unimodular. The elementary height-one proof is correct: after sending a primitive edge to \((1,0)\) and writing the third vertex as \((s,t)\), \(t\ge2\) makes the height-one section
\[
[s/t,(s+t-1)/t]
\]
contain \(\lceil s/t\rceil\). This is a forbidden extra lattice point. Hence all three determinants equal one, and the three vertices normalize to \(e_1,e_2,-e_1-e_2\).

6. The exclusion of every further point uses an exact convex combination. Permuting the three normalized vertices puts a further integer point at \((i,j)\), \(i\ge j\ge0\), \(i+j\ge2\). If \(j\ge1\), then
\[
(1,1)=\frac{(i,j)+(j-1)e_1+(i-1)e_2}{i+j-1},
\]
which creates the opposite pair \((1,1),(-1,-1)\) through zero. If \(j=0\), then \(2e_1\) lies in the polygon and the hyperedge with endpoints \(0,2e_1\) violates isolation. Thus the polygon has exactly the four Fano-triangle points.

7. Those four points have distinct parities and no midpoint hyperedges. The three nonmissing points therefore cannot be one rank-two connected component. This is the required contradiction.

For an affine-rank-two component in \(\mathbb Z^n\), its affine span carries the saturated lattice \(\Lambda=V\cap\mathbb Z^n\). Ambient even differences are exactly \(2\Lambda\), since an ambient integer half-difference remains in \(V\). A lattice basis therefore preserves precisely the relevant parity and midpoint relations. The planar proof applies without changing any mixed measure.

The proof is self-contained apart from elementary finite-dimensional lattice basis and Bezout facts. No computational screen, Pick formula, general-position hypothesis, or classification of hollow polygons is needed.
